title: Within-object response variance used more dimensions in IT than V4 in public recordings from two macaques
abstract: We tested why an increased object variance share did not produce total response compression in a public macaque data set. We used four disjoint repeat groups to estimate object and within-object covariance moments in V4 and IT. In monkey Chabo, with 30 sites per area, the object share rose from 0.158 to 0.354. Object participation ratio showed no clear change, including with disjoint images. Within-object participation ratio rose from 4.58 to 7.47 and total participation ratio from 4.57 to 6.04. A share-only counterfactual predicted a decrease of 0.49 dimensions; changed geometry added 1.97 dimensions. In monkey Tito, with 16 sites per area, within-object dimension also rose, by 1.75, but the object share difference and share-only effect were uncertain. Raw-rate controls gave similar results. Ranges describe 200 site, image and repeat subsamples, not uncertainty across animals. Thus the macaque absence of total compression includes a spread of within-object signals, while an expanded object identity code was not resolved. This describes one public assembly and does not identify a circuit mechanism or explain mouse compression. Original code, aggregate results, a figure, source hashes and retrieval instructions support reproduction.

display.caption: Chabo, 30 sites per area. Object share increases, but within-object signals use more dimensions in IT. Curves exchange variance share while keeping covariance geometry fixed. Bars and bands are 95 percent subsample stability ranges, not animal population confidence intervals.
